title: Difficult people in the rule
hookLine: a practice for the hard ones: Beruriah told Rabbi Meir to pray for the end of the sins, not the sinners
tomorrow: why did an old man run, in the heat, to three strangers?

cards: Every building seems to have one: the neighbor with the bass at two in the morning, the one who leaves notes.

The Talmud tells of Rabbi Meir, a great teacher, who had neighbors like that, rough men who made his life miserable. And one day, the text says plainly, he prayed that they would die. His wife, Beruriah, heard him.

teach.b: Beruriah didn't scold. She argued from a verse, the way the rabbis do. You're leaning on the psalm, she said: "Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth."
But read the Hebrew closely. The word can be read as sins, not sinners. Let the sins end.

teach.h: LET THE WICKED BE NO MORE.
teach.b: And look at the end of the verse: "and let the wicked be no more." Once the sins are gone, there are no wicked left.
So pray for them to turn. Rabbi Meir prayed for them, the Talmud says, and they turned.
The Jewish teaching inside it: Judaism holds that people can return, teshuvah, and a prayer about an enemy can aim at the wrong, not the person.
For a rule of life, that's a practice for the hard ones: one line, kept on hand, that hopes for the harm to end and the person to turn.

how: Jewish teaching on teshuvah, returning, holds that a wrongdoer can turn. A rule of life, on any path, can include one short practice or line for the people who are hardest to be around.

games.q: what does “difficult people in the rule” mean?
o: a set of rules difficult people must follow around you
a short practice for the hard people, hoping they turn
a list of people you've decided never to see again

p: prayed his rough neighbors would die
once sins end, no wicked remain

s: Beruriah told Rabbi Meir he was wrong to pray at all about his neighbors
she told him to pray differently: for the sins to end and for them to turn.
in the Talmud's story, the rough neighbors turned after Rabbi Meir prayed for them
he prayed for them to return, and they did.

games.q: a coworker keeps taking credit for others' work. your friend wants a line for her rule. by Beruriah's reading, which fits?
o: may the taking stop, and may he become someone who shares the credit.
may he finally get caught and lose that job for good.
may I never have to think about him again.
games.why: Beruriah read the psalm as a prayer against the sins, not the sinners: when the wrong ends, the person can turn.

practice: Write one line for the hard ones in your rule, something you can come back to before you meet them. Let it hope for the harm to end, not for the person to be gone. Then sit with one hard person's face in mind, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Difficult people in the rule: a short practice for the hard ones, hoping their harm ends and they turn, as Beruriah taught Rabbi Meir.

orig.note: Hebrew, Jewish teaching: 'return', turning back from wrongdoing.

carryVoice: Your line: the hard ones. Pray against the sins, not the sinners, said Beruriah. A week of others, gathered in.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 10a (Rabbi Meir, the rough neighbors, Beruriah's reading of Psalm 104:35)

sources.q: Let the sinners be consumed out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more.
